newsitem.title: FRANCE: France "outraged" at TV film on Srebrenica.
newsitem.headline: France "outraged" at TV film on Srebrenica.

text.p: The French defence ministry hit out on Thursday at a television programme which effectively accused a top French general of allowing the massacre of thousands of Bosnians in the town of Srebrenica last year.
"Defence Minister (Charles) Millon is absolutely outraged by these baseless accusations against General (Bernard) Janvier," spokesman Pierre Servent told a press briefing.
Servent was answering questions after the showing last week of a film on one of the most horrific episodes of the 43-month Bosnian civil war.

It contended that Janvier, then U.N. commander in former Yugoslavia, refrained from ordering up air strikes to defend Srebrenica from the Serbs in exchange for the release of U.N. peacekeepers then held hostage.

Servent said it was on record that France was the driving power behind the creation, after Srebrenica, of an international "Rapid Reaction Force" which, together with NATO aircraft, effectively halted Serb advances and brought the war to an end.

Ilan Ziv, co-producer and director of the film, told Reuters from New York: "It's very easy to call the film baseless. I challenge Mr Millon to come up with his proof because we've come up with our proof.
"We have spoken to people who were at meetings between Janvier and (Bosnian Serb commander Radko) Mladic and we've seen all the minutes of key meetings concerning air strikes on Srebrenica."
Bosnian Serbs captured Srebrenica, then supposed to be a U.N. "safe area", in July 1995. Thousands of Moslem men went missing and are generally believed to have been killed and buried in mass graves.
Janvier refused to be interviewed for the programme, produced by Tamouz Media, Reuters Television and Point du Jour.

The documentary, based on interviews, secret documents and transcripts of radio intercepts, said Janvier and U.N. special representative Yasushi Akashi failed to pass on clear warnings that Srebrenica, defended by some 400 Dutch U.N. soldiers, was about to fall.

French army officers have complained privately that their government prevented Janvier from answering the accusations against him because his statements would supposedly have created a row between France and the United Nations.
Janvier, who until the Srebrenica episode was widely believed to be earmarked as next commander of the French army, was passed over for the post when it became free this summer.
